title: Banning Sugary Food at Checkouts Cuts Soda Sales
paragraphs: Many supermarkets place candy, chocolate and soda right next to the checkout, where customers often grab them on impulse while waiting in line. Now, a new study suggests that removing these items from checkouts can lead to a significant drop in soda sales.

The study, published in the journal The Lancet Public Health in September 2026, was led by researchers from Boston University and the University of California, Davis. It examined the effects of a policy introduced in Berkeley, California. In 2021, Berkeley became the first city in the world to ban the display of sugary drinks and snacks at checkout lanes. The rule became fully enforceable on January 1, 2022. However, stores are still allowed to sell these products in other parts of the store.

The researchers analyzed sales data from 71 stores, including supermarkets, drugstores and large discount stores, in Berkeley and three other California cities without the policy: Davis, Oakland and Sacramento. They tracked sales from March 2019 to December 2023.

The results showed that soda sales in Berkeley fell substantially after the policy was introduced and enforced. Sales of small packages of candy also fell significantly in supermarkets. At the same time, sales of healthier, lower-sugar snacks, such as small packs of nuts and seeds, increased.

However, the effects were not the same everywhere. Supermarkets, which followed the rules most closely, saw the largest drops in sales of sugary products. In contrast, drugstores, which followed the rules the least, saw no drop in candy or soda sales. In addition, overall candy sales did not fall, possibly because stores could move candy to other areas.

According to Justin White, one of the study's lead authors, it is critical for cities to actively enforce such policies. Jennifer Falbe of UC Davis, the study's senior author, added that no single policy can solve the problems with the food system on its own.
Eating too much sugar is linked to diabetes, heart disease and tooth decay.
